name: Structured Output and Function Calling
intent: Get output a program can rely on from a model that writes free text, and let a model ask your code to do things, without trusting what it says.
scenario: An order-status assistant must hand a program a JSON object with an integer order id and a status. Sometimes the model wraps the JSON in friendly text, sometimes it writes the id as a string, and sometimes it asks for a tool the app never offered.
problem: A language model writes text, and a program needs data: valid JSON, the right fields, the right types. A model that is asked nicely for JSON usually complies and sometimes does not, and a parser fails on the exception. Function calling raises the stakes, because the output is no longer displayed but acted on. Whatever the model writes in a tool call is untrusted input, and it can be malformed, wrong or the result of an attack.

howItWorks.title: Ask, then validate
howItWorks.text: The simplest approach describes the format in the prompt and checks the result with a parser and a schema. A failure is detected, not prevented. The failure can be syntax (not JSON at all) or shape (the id is a string, a field is missing).

howItWorks.title: Retry with the error
howItWorks.text: On failure the application asks again, ideally including the error message, up to a small limit. If a call fails with probability p, the chance that all of n tries fail is p to the power n, so a few retries fix most cases, at the cost of extra calls, delay and tokens.

howItWorks.title: Constrained decoding prevents invalid output
howItWorks.text: Instead of checking afterwards, the decoder removes the tokens that would break the grammar or schema before the next token is chosen. Willard and Louf describe generation as transitions of a finite-state machine, with an index over the vocabulary that finds the valid next tokens quickly, with little overhead. The output then always has the right syntax.

howItWorks.title: Valid is not the same as correct
howItWorks.text: Constraints guarantee the shape of the output, not its truth. A perfectly formed object can hold the wrong order id or a made-up status. Business checks, such as does this order exist, still belong to the application.

howItWorks.title: Function calling: the model asks, the app acts
howItWorks.text: The application describes the tools it offers: names and argument schemas. The model replies with a call, a name and arguments, instead of text. The application runs the tool and sends the result back, and the model continues. The model never runs anything itself.

howItWorks.title: Treat every call as untrusted input
howItWorks.text: Check the name against an allow-list, validate the arguments against the schema, enforce permissions as if a user had typed the request, and make write operations safe to repeat. Text in documents or web pages the model has read can steer its calls, so never hand it a tool that it must not be allowed to use.

pros: Programs can use model output without fragile string handling
Validation and retries make failures visible and recoverable
Constrained decoding removes a whole class of syntax errors
Function calling lets a model use live data and take actions through code you control
cons: A valid structure can still hold wrong content, so correctness needs separate checks
Retries add latency and cost, and a bad prompt can fail the same way every time
Tight constraints can force the model to fit its answer into the format, even when the format is wrong for it
Tool calls are an attack surface: a model can be talked into calling the wrong thing
whenToUse: A program, not a person, consumes the model's output
The model needs to look something up or act through your own code
You can write down the format as a schema and check it
whenNotToUse: Do not use free text parsing with regular expressions when a schema is available
Do not expose a tool the model should never be allowed to use, and rely on the prompt to stop it
Do not skip business validation because the output is well formed
pitfalls: Parsing the first brace in a reply and ignoring text around it, or the reverse
Retrying forever, so that one stubborn failure becomes a large bill
Treating a schema-valid result as proof that the answer is right
Running a model's tool call without checking permissions, arguments or that a write is safe to repeat

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Describes the format and the tools, checks everything it receives, and runs the tools.

roles.label: Model
roles.description: Writes text, or a structured reply that names a tool and its arguments.

roles.label: Schema or grammar
roles.description: States what a valid output looks like. Used to validate, or to constrain decoding.

roles.label: Tool
roles.description: Your own function that does the real work. Only allowed tools can be called.

sources.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models

quiz.question: An application parses the model's reply as JSON, and it crashes in about 5 percent of calls because the model adds friendly text around the JSON. What is the best fix?
options: Remove everything before the first brace, since the model always puts the JSON last
Use a structured output mode or constrained decoding, or validate the reply and retry with the error message
Raise the temperature, so that the model varies its answers and sometimes writes plain JSON
Ask the model more politely in the prompt, and accept that it will still fail occasionally
quiz.explanation: Syntax problems are best prevented by constraining the decoder, or at least detected by a parser and retried with the error. Cutting at the first brace breaks when the text comes after the JSON or contains a brace, a higher temperature adds randomness, and politeness is not a guarantee.

quiz.question: A team uses constrained decoding, and the JSON now always parses. But the 'total' field sometimes holds a wrong amount. Why?
options: The decoder is faulty, because constrained decoding is supposed to prevent any wrong values
The model ignores the schema for numbers, so numeric fields cannot be constrained at all
The constraint was too loose, and a stricter schema would make the amounts correct
A grammar guarantees the shape of the output, not that its content is true, so the amount still needs a separate check
quiz.explanation: Constraints control which tokens may be written, so syntax and types are guaranteed. They say nothing about whether a number is right. Check it against the source of truth, for example by recomputing the total in the application.

quiz.question: A model's function call names a tool, delete_all, that the application never offered. What should the application do?
options: Refuse the call, because it is not on the allow-list, and return an error to the model
Run the call, because the model has probably been trained to call only sensible tools
Run the closest matching tool that is on the allow-list, and hide the difference from the user
Ask the model to confirm that it wants to call the tool, and run it if it says yes
quiz.explanation: A tool call is untrusted input. Only names on the allow-list may run, and an unknown one should be refused and reported back. The model's own confirmation proves nothing, and silently substituting another tool hides a problem that should be visible.
